item.title: Steve Jermy: Ukraine, Europe's Suicide & Global Energy Crisis
item.description: Royal Navy Commodore Steve Jermy commanded warships in the 5th Destroyer Squadron and Britain's Fleet Air Arm.
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
Royal Navy Commodore Steve Jermy commanded warships in the 5th Destroyer Squadron and Britain's Fleet Air Arm. He served in the Falklands War and in the Adriatic for the Bosnian and Kosovo campaigns. Then retired after an operational tour, in 2007, as Strategy Director in the British Embassy in Afghanistan. He is the author of the book: "Strategy for Action: Using Force Wisely in the 21st Century".

item.title: Why Russia's Peace Deal Will Constantly Change
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
Russia has repeatedly warned NATO that any future peace deal will become more unfavorable with each passing day. Why? NATO has pushed for a long war as it can weaken a strategic rival by fighting with Ukrainians. The US walked back its own proposal made in Alaska, and European leaders still boycott basic diplomacy.

However, territorial changes are problematic for NATO and are therefore one of the few incentives to make peace. If Russia offers the same peace deal six months from now, it only communicates that NATO can spend six more months attacking Russian military and economic targets without any costs to itself.

Even the RAND paper from 2019 on “Extending Russia” recognized that it was in NATO’s interest to escalate the conflict in Donbas to compel Russia to devote more resources, yet it warned that the breakout of an all-out war would be unfavorable if strategic territory ended up under Russian control.

If we do not criminalize honesty about NATO and Russian strategic interests and options, then the Russian peace proposals make sense. Russia will demand the original Istanbul deal (April 2022), which would have restored Ukrainian sovereignty, as the foundation for any future deal - plus incrementally more territorial demands the longer the war goes on.
